lesson-1-sphere|Define the sphere placem.text: Let’s pause here. Start by ghosting four light marks where the sphere will sit. These four marks define the size and position. Leave breathing room around the edges of your paper.

lesson-1-sphere|Measure left and right|4.text: Let’s pause here. Hold your pencil horizontally. Measure from the center to the left mark, then to the right mark. They should be equal — if not, adjust.

lesson-1-sphere|Measure top and bottom|8.text: Let’s pause here. Rotate your pencil vertically. Compare distance from center to top, then to bottom. Equal distances = a true sphere, not an oval.

lesson-1-sphere|Find the diagonal points.text: Let’s pause here. Use the same pencil-radius to locate four diagonal guide points (NE, NW, SE, SW). These eight points together define the circle.

lesson-1-sphere|See the full framework|1.text: Let’s pause here. This is the scaffolding underneath every well-drawn sphere. The cross gives you center. The eight points give you the curve. Trust the structure.

lesson-1-sphere|Cut with straight tangen.text: Let’s pause here. Beginner mistake: drawing a curve straight away. Instead, connect your eight points with short straight lines first. A circle is just many small straight cuts.

lesson-1-sphere|Refine into a clean curv.text: Let’s pause here. Once your tangent cuts are right, gently round the corners. Don't force perfection — let the curve emerge from the geometry you built.

lesson-1-sphere|Erase the cutting lines|.text: Let’s pause here. After cutting the sphere with straight tangents, use your eraser to clean away the leftover construction lines. This refinement makes the outer edge feel round, smooth, and natural — not geometric.

lesson-1-sphere|Cast shadow + sphere tog.text: Let’s pause here. Draw the cast shadow at the same time as you finish the sphere. They're not two separate elements — they're one connected structure. The shadow grounds the sphere; the sphere casts the shadow.

lesson-1-sphere|Mark the terminator line.text: Let’s pause here. As soon as the form is drawn, use the terminator line to clearly separate the light side from the shadow side. This single line is what makes a sphere read as three-dimensional.

lesson-1-sphere|Strengthen the terminato.text: Let’s pause here. Return to the terminator line and reinforce it. Strengthening this boundary is what creates strong contrast between the light side and the shadow side — and that contrast is what gives the sphere its volume.

lesson-1-sphere|Sharpen the shadow contr.text: Let’s pause here. Now move to the cast shadow below the sphere and strengthen its main contrast line. Making the shadow side firmly darker than the light side is what completes the illusion of form sitting in space.

lesson-1-sphere|Tone inside the terminat.text: Let’s pause here. Begin laying tone strictly within the terminator. Don't let your pencil cross over into the light side. This boundary is what gives the sphere its volume.

lesson-1-sphere|Strengthen the terminato.text: Let’s pause here. Return to the terminator line after the overall tone is in. Push it darker — this line should always remain the deepest, most focused dark on the form.

lesson-1-sphere|Tone the shadow as one f.text: Let’s pause here. Tone the cast shadow alongside the sphere, not separately. Sphere and shadow belong to the same value family — they should be developed together so they feel unified, not pasted together.

lesson-1-sphere|Anchor the sphere to the.text: Let’s pause here. Once the cast shadow is filled, return to the area where the sphere meets the surface and push that contrast hard. This is the darkest part of the cast shadow — it's what makes the sphere feel grounded, not floating.

lesson-1-sphere|Shadow gradation \u2014.text: Let’s pause here. Finish by strengthening the shadow nearest to us, then gradate it lighter as it moves away. This near-to-far gradation stretches the perception of space — the shadow becomes the tool that pulls the eye into depth.

lesson-1-sphere|Build the light-gray hal.text: Let’s pause here. This is the halftone area — a band of value that extends from the terminator into the light side. Wrap it gently around the whole sphere. Switch to a lighter pencil (HB or 2H) — this is not a line, it's an entire surface that helps the light side transition naturally.

lesson-1-sphere|Cross-hatch to unify the.text: Let’s pause here. When you tone over your own strokes in the same direction, the result can feel rigid. Mrs. Dawn now adds strokes in the opposite direction — cross-hatching. This blending pass unifies the earlier tones into a softer, more continuous surface.

lesson-1-sphere|Soften the terminator in.text: Let’s pause here. A common mistake: drawing the terminator as a sharp, rigid line or block. Mrs. Dawn pushes that area repeatedly — not just darkening it, but also blending it gradually into the shadow side. The terminator should feel like a natural transition, not a wall.

lesson-1-sphere|It's a terminator BAND,.text: Let’s pause here. Look carefully — Mrs. Dawn defines a clear terminator AREA, not a terminator line. This band acts as a bridge between the light side and the shadow side. It's what makes the sphere pop forward in 3D, and it's the key visual link between the two value zones.

lesson-1-sphere|Switch to 2B for stronge.text: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn explicitly switches to a 2B pencil. The HB has carried you this far; the 2B will let you push the values that need to feel firmer and richer.

lesson-1-sphere|Radiate from the termina.text: Let’s pause here. With 2B, Mrs. Dawn strengthens transitions in both directions — from the terminator toward the light side, and from the terminator toward the dark side. This radiating gradient is what gives the sphere strong perspective. She also strengthens the cast shadow with the same pencil.

lesson-1-sphere|Bring out the blender|31.text: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn introduces a blending tool — a blending stump if you have one, or a tissue or napkin works fine. This tool unifies and softens all the tones you've built up. The drawing should feel more like a smooth surface than a series of pencil strokes.

lesson-1-sphere|Follow your stroke direc.text: Let’s pause here. Important: when blending, follow the direction of your pencil strokes. Sweep gently in the same direction. Do not press hard, and do not blend randomly across the surface — that creates a muddy, dirty drawing. Light, directional sweeps only.

lesson-1-sphere|Optional: re-touch with.text: Let’s pause here. This step is optional but recommended. Mrs. Dawn returns to the HB pencil and gently presses the strongest tones back into the paper. This subtly tightens the whole drawing and makes it feel more natural — less like raw pencil, more like a unified surface.

lesson-3-cube|Position your drawing on t.text: Let’s pause here. Notice how Mrs. Dawn places small marks for the cube's four outer edges before she draws anything else. The distance from these marks to the edge of the paper matters — too close to the edge feels cramped, too centered feels stiff. Take a moment: do you have your paper ready, with room around where the cube will sit?

lesson-3-cube|Use your pencil as a measu.text: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn holds her pencil at arm's length to measure the cube's height. This is one of the most important habits in observational drawing — your pencil becomes a ruler. Try holding your pencil this way now: arm fully extended, one eye closed. Mark the height before you commit to any lines.

lesson-3-cube|The top plane \u2014 paral.text: Let’s pause here. This is where most students go wrong. The top of the cube tilts away from us — but you need to draw it parallel first, then gently apply perspective. Don't try to "see the angle" right away. Draw the top edges horizontal, then carefully tilt them inward. Look at Mrs. Dawn's example: notice how subtle the perspective actually is.

lesson-3-cube|See through the cube \u201.text: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn draws the cube as if it were transparent — showing the edges you can't actually see. This isn't for show. Understanding the internal framework helps you feel the cube's 3D space. The back corners must align with the front corners. If your hidden edges look wrong, the visible ones will too.

lesson-3-cube|Perspective lines: paralle.text: Let’s pause here. Same rule as the top plane — keep your perspective lines (and any diagonal/background lines) parallel first. THEN gently bring them inward toward the vanishing point. Going straight to "angled" without "parallel" first makes the cube look wonky. Slow it down. Parallel first. Tilt second.

lesson-3-cube|4B: Start from the darkest.text: Let’s pause here. Start with a 4B pencil and build the darkest plane first. Keep all of your strokes moving in one direction so the shading feels clean and organized.

lesson-3-cube|Change direction|23.text: Let’s pause here. Now change direction and add a second layer over the first shading. This helps build a smoother transition and gives the form stronger depth.

lesson-3-cube|Fully apply the dark plane.text: Let’s pause here. Now fully cover the dark plane. Try to keep the tone even across the whole side so it feels complete and well controlled.

lesson-3-cube|Strengthen the light-dark.text: Let’s pause here. Strengthen the edge between the light side and the dark side. This boundary is what helps the cube feel sharper and more three-dimensional.

lesson-3-cube|Add the cast shadow|87.text: Let’s pause here. Now add the cast shadow. Keep the strokes moving in one direction here too, so the shadow stays clean and controlled.

lesson-3-cube|2B: Add the light-gray pla.text: Let’s pause here. Switch to a 2B pencil and shade the light gray plane with a lighter touch. Create contrast, but keep the transition into the dark plane soft.

lesson-3-cube|HB: Unify the surface|182.text: Let’s pause here. Use an HB pencil to lightly sweep over the surface. This helps clean up rough strokes and makes the tone feel more unified.

lesson-3-cube|Blend lightly|198.text: Let’s pause here. Now use a tissue or a blender to soften the graphite. Blend lightly so the tones transition smoothly, while the shape of the cube stays clear.

lesson-3-cube|Edge dissolves \u2014 top.text: Let’s pause here. Watch how the outer edge is slowly disappearing into the background. It no longer reads as a separate line. And notice the top plane — by darkening the background around it, the top has become much brighter without being touched.

lesson-3-cube|Strengthen the shadow|99.text: Let’s pause here. Now Mrs. Dawn strengthens the shadow area. By pushing the shadow darker, the contrast between light and dark becomes stronger — and that contrast is what makes the form feel three-dimensional.

lesson-3-cube|Return to the terminator l.text: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn goes back to the terminator line — the boundary between light and shadow — and reinforces it. This is what creates the strongest sense of three-dimensional form. The darker the terminator, the more the cube pops.

lesson-3-cube|Natural tonal transition|2.text: Let’s pause here. Look at the full cube now. From left to right, from top to bottom, the tone transitions naturally from dark to light. This gradual flow is what makes the form feel unified and real.

lesson-3-cube|Blend to unify|219.text: Let’s pause here. Now blend the surface gently. A blending stump, tissue, or cotton bud all work. Follow the direction of your strokes and sweep very lightly. This softens the transitions and unifies the whole surface.

lesson-5-cylinder|Measure left & right w.text: Let’s pause here. Just like we practiced before — use your pencil as a measuring tool. Compare left to right so the cylinder begins with a stable, balanced frame from the very first stroke.

lesson-5-cylinder|Mark top, bottom, left.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher places dots above, below, and on each side. These four points define how much of the page the cylinder will fill. Check the gap to the paper edge — too big or too small and the composition fails.

lesson-5-cylinder|Box the cylinder in a.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher draws a long rectangle around where the cylinder will sit. This rectangle gives the cylinder a clear, direct answer for its size — no guessing.

lesson-5-cylinder|Check that top & botto.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher finds a point and measures with the pencil — checking whether the top section matches the area of the bottom. Equal proportions = a believable cylinder.

lesson-5-cylinder|Frame where the front.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher draws specific guide frames at the top and bottom. These tell you exactly where the front curve should arc through. With this scaffolding, your pencil moves with confidence.

lesson-5-cylinder|Cut with straight tang.text: Let’s pause here. Just like with the sphere — circles and ellipses are very hard for beginners. The teacher uses straight tangent cuts first to find the right angles, then softens them into a curve.

lesson-5-cylinder|Find the bottom curve.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher locates the starting points for the bottom ellipse. Find the highest and lowest points of the curve — and they must be perfectly left-right symmetric.

lesson-5-cylinder|Keep top & bottom curv.text: Let’s pause here. The bottom curve is almost finished. Common mistake: students draw it too flat. The top and bottom curves must arc downward in parallel — if either becomes too flat, the perspective breaks.

lesson-5-cylinder|Start the terminator w.text: Let’s pause here. Switch to a 2B pencil. The terminator on a cylinder runs vertically — let your pencil strokes follow that direction, sweeping down along the form. Keep it light at first; you can deepen it later.

lesson-5-cylinder|Sketch the cast shadow.text: Let’s pause here. Now draw the cast shadow on the table — its outline follows the shape the cylinder casts on the surface. Develop the terminator and the shadow together. They belong to one connected system, not two separate things.

lesson-5-cylinder|Rough-shade the dark s.text: Let’s pause here. Take a 2B pencil and lay down a quick pass of tone across the dark side, vertical strokes following the cylinder's direction. This is rough shading — it doesn't need to be pretty. Just lay it in fast and uniform.

lesson-5-cylinder|Always develop the sha.text: Let’s pause here. The cylinder and its shadow always develop together — never separately. Use the same stroke direction so the eye reads them as one unified scene.

lesson-5-cylinder|Strengthen the shadow.text: Let’s pause here. Return to the cast shadow and deepen it. This stronger contrast anchors the cylinder to the surface and gives the whole drawing more visual punch.

lesson-5-cylinder|Add horizontal strokes.text: Let’s pause here. Even though we strengthened the terminator, it shouldn't look stiff. Add horizontal strokes across it now — these will become the bridge to the light side later, making the eventual transition feel natural.

lesson-5-cylinder|Blend with paper, foll.text: Let’s pause here. Just like with the sphere and cube, take a piece of rolled paper (or tissue) and blend along the direction of your strokes. This unifies the tone without losing the form direction.

lesson-5-cylinder|Switch to 3B \u2014 pu.text: Let’s pause here. Now switch to a 3B pencil. Push the value contrast further — but keep the strokes going the same direction. No messy criss-crossing.

lesson-5-cylinder|Vertical strokes turn.text: Let’s pause here. Lay more vertical strokes through the dark side. The terminator stops reading as a single line and becomes a band of value — that's what makes the form feel three-dimensional.

lesson-5-cylinder|Horizontal strokes aga.text: Let’s pause here. Add another pass of horizontal strokes. We're building the bridge between dark and light — the gentler the transition, the more believable the form.

lesson-5-cylinder|Shadow \u2014 denser,.text: Let’s pause here. Return to the cast shadow one more time. This time the strokes are denser, more deliberate, more controlled. The whole drawing becomes cleaner and more crisp.

lesson-5-cylinder|Switch to HB or 2H for.text: Let’s pause here. Switch to HB or 2H — pick based on how heavy your touch is. Heavy hand → 2H. Light hand → HB. Lightly start hatching the half-light area with vertical, parallel strokes.

lesson-5-cylinder|Build the bridge: dark.text: Let’s pause here. This is the key move: the gradation from dark to light. Use HB if your touch is light, 2H if your touch is heavy. Smooth, continuous transition wraps the cylinder.

lesson-5-cylinder|Use 2H to refine detai.text: Let’s pause here. For more refined detail work, switch to 2H. The lighter graphite lets you sharpen and define without darkening areas you don't want darker.

lesson-5-cylinder|Diagonal strokes on th.text: Let’s pause here. Bring 2B back. Build the gradation in the dark side with diagonal strokes going up. The change in stroke direction reinforces the form's curve.

lesson-5-cylinder|Light side gets 2H tre.text: Let’s pause here. Use 2H to add the finishing touches on the light side. Strokes stay parallel and gentle — this is the lightest value zone.

lesson-5-cylinder|Outer edge: drawn but.text: Let’s pause here. The outer (far) edge needs tone, but it shouldn't be as hard as the terminator. Remember: the terminator is in front, the outer edge is behind. The closer thing is sharper; the farther thing is softer.

lesson-5-cylinder|Clean diagonal shading.text: Let’s pause here. Use diagonal strokes for a clean shading pass. You should see a tidy, parallel band of hatching — this is the controlled finish that separates a polished drawing from a sketch.

lesson-5-cylinder|Switch back to 2B|507.text: Let’s pause here. Switch back to 2B to add some final depth where needed. Brief and surgical — only the spots that need pushing.

lesson-5-cylinder|Final blending pass|56.text: Let’s pause here. Final blending — use paper or tissue to unify the surface one last time. After this, the dark side of the cylinder reads as a continuous, three-dimensional form.

still-life-2a-glass-structure|Start with.text: Let’s pause here. A light centerline helps you compare the left and right sides of the bottle. Keep it straight, then check both sides against it.

still-life-2a-glass-structure|Measure pr.text: Let’s pause here. Compare the height and width before adding detail. Small tick marks help you keep the bottle and cup in proportion.

still-life-2a-glass-structure|Straight l.text: Let’s pause here. Use light, straight construction lines to find the big shape first. You can soften the corners once the proportions look right.

still-life-2a-glass-structure|Straight e.text: Let’s pause here. Look at the sloping edges of the bottle. Compare their angles with your pencil before refining the curved outline.

still-life-1a-star-balloon-structure|Fin.text: Let’s pause here. The teacher is finding the direction and overall shape before adding any shading. Notice the tilted guide lines. Compare their angles, and keep your construction marks light.

still-life-1a-star-balloon-structure|Tur.text: Let’s pause here. Pause to compare the outline with the finished balloon beside the video. The edges bend inward between the points. Use gentle curves instead of making every edge a straight line.

still-life-1a-star-balloon-structure|Sep.text: Let’s pause here. Look closely at the rim just inside the balloon outline. This seam is separate from the outer edge. Keep that narrow space visible; it will help the balloon feel like inflated foil.

still-life-1a-star-balloon-structure|Let.text: Let’s pause here. These small inward curves describe folds in the foil. Notice how they turn from the rim toward the centre. Draw the folds you can see, keeping them light before the shading begins.
